speaker: Doctor
text: Hello, I am Dr. Agent. Please describe your neck swelling in detail: how long has it been present, is it painful, and has it changed in size recently?

speaker: Patient
text: 50-year-old male. The patient reports a progressively increasing swelling on the nape of his neck for 2 months. He denies having a fever, pain, or any discharge from the swelling. He mentions a history of colon cancer for which he underwent colectomy at the age of 43. He also has a history of type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, and osteoarthritis of the left knee. He takes insulin glargine, metformin, enalapril, and naproxen.

speaker: Doctor
text:
That history of colon cancer is very concerning given the location of the swelling at the nape of your neck; has this mass been increasing in size rapidly over the last two months, and have you noticed any difficulty swallowing or breathing?

REQUEST TEST: Neck_Ultrasound.
REQUEST IMAGES: Neck_Soft_Tissue_Swelling.

speaker: Measurement
text: RESULTS: Ultrasound of the Neck shows a well-circumscribed lesion in the subcutaneous tissue suggestive of a cystic nature.

speaker: Doctor
text:
The ultrasound indicates a cystic lesion, but given your history of colon cancer, we must rule out metastasis. Does the mass feel fluctuant or firm to the touch, and have you noticed any changes in the skin overlying the swelling, such as redness or warmth?

REQUEST TEST: CT_Scan_Neck_With_Contrast.

speaker: Measurement
text: RESULTS: CT Scan of the Neck with Contrast shows a well-defined, hypodense, cystic lesion in the subcutaneous tissue of the posterior neck with thin walls and no evidence of internal solid components, calcifications, or vascular invasion. No suspicious lymphadenopathy or metastatic disease is identified in the neck, thyroid, or mediastinum. The lesion demonstrates no contrast enhancement, consistent with a benign cystic structure such as a sebaceous cyst or epidermal inclusion cyst.

speaker: Doctor
text:
DIAGNOSIS READY: Benign Epidermal Inclusion Cyst (Sebaceous Cyst).

The imaging confirms a benign, non-metastatic cystic lesion, ruling out recurrent colon cancer or other malignancies. No further tests are required at this time.
